images.title: Doubling doubles the HCF
images.purpose: Show that doubling both numbers adds one extra 2 to each factorisation, and that this 2 joins the HCF.
images.composition: Two blocks stacked vertically, the original pair on top and the doubled pair below, joined by one grey downward arrow, centred with wide margins.
exact_structure: Top block (teal #0072B2 text) has 3 lines: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3, then 18 = 2 × 3 × 3, then HCF = 2 × 3 = 6.
One grey #6B7280 downward arrow between the blocks with the label double both beside it.
Bottom block (amber #E69F00 text) has 3 lines: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3, then 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, then HCF = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.
In each of the 3 bottom lines the first 2 after the equals sign (the extra 2) is drawn in reddish purple #CC79A7 inside a small circle: exactly 3 circled 2s.
The two HCF lines (6 and 12) are in bold.
rejection: any factorisation that does not multiply back to its number
a top HCF other than 6 or a bottom HCF other than 12
more or fewer than 3 circled reddish purple 2s
images.takeaway: When both numbers are doubled, each gets an extra 2, that 2 is common, so the HCF doubles.
images.description: 12 and 18 factorised with HCF 6, an arrow down, then 24 and 36 factorised with the extra 2 circled and HCF 12.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on doubling both numbers.
images.teaching_notes: Point to the circled 2 in each doubled number, then to the circled 2 in the new HCF.

image_decisions.why: Seeing the one extra 2 travel into the HCF is the whole reason the HCF doubles.
